verses.note: Whatever its original horizon, the verse refuses to treat Sheol as the last word for one who belongs to God. Interpreters differ on whether David hoped for rescue from an early death or for life beyond death; the psalm's language opens toward the second.

Luke describes death as the spirit leaving and life as the spirit returning, the same language he uses when Jesus commits his spirit to the Father (23:46) and Stephen asks Jesus to receive his (Acts 7:59). The verse supports the biblical picture of the person continuing beyond death, though it says nothing about where the girl's spirit had been.

Amillennial readers see in this verse the state of believers between death and resurrection: the souls of the martyrs are alive with Christ and share his reign now, while their bodies wait for the resurrection at the end. On this reading the verse answers the cry of 6:9-11 by showing the martyrs already enthroned.
